name: Bindable
first: A property wrapper for a view's property that holds an observable class, which makes a binding to any property of that class.

dependsOn.why: A bindable property holds an observable class, and its bindings read and write that class's properties.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The class `Trip` is observable, as `Trip` is on the page of Observable.

dependsOn.why: A bindable property makes bindings, which a view passes to another view that changes the value.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The property `count` in `Adder` is a binding, as `nights` in `NightsEditor` is on the page of Binding.

what.is: A bindable property is a property of a view marked `@Bindable`, which holds an observable class. A dollar sign before it and a property's name after it, as `$trip.nights`, make a binding to that property of the object.
what.afterExample: The view `Adder` changes a number through a binding. The view `TripEditor` gives it a binding to `nights` of the trip, so when `Adder` adds 1, the trip's `nights` becomes 4, as line 27 prints.
what.problem: Controls and editors take a binding for the value they change. A state property gives a binding with a dollar sign, but a view that is given an observable class holds it in a plain property, which gives no binding. A bindable property gives a binding to each property of the class.
what.how: The type `Bindable` is a property wrapper that SwiftUI provides. Its projected value, read with `$trip`, makes a binding for the property named after it. Reading that binding reads `nights` of the trip, and writing it sets `nights`, which the observable class reports as any other change.

when.text: Use it in a view that is given an observable class and must pass a binding to one of its properties, such as to an editor or a control.
Don't use it in a view that only reads the object. A plain property is enough there, because reading the object's properties needs no binding.

parts.name: The bindable property `trip`, line 17
parts.text: The attribute `@Bindable` makes `trip` a wrapped property of `Bindable`, a property wrapper that SwiftUI provides. Its wrapped value is the `Trip` that line 24 passes in.

parts.name: The dollar sign, in `$trip`, line 19
parts.text: A dollar sign before `trip` reads the projected value of `Bindable`, which can make a binding to each property of the trip.

parts.name: The property `nights`, after `$trip`, line 19
parts.text: The name `nights` after `$trip` makes a binding to `nights` of the trip. Line 19 passes it to `count` of `Adder`.

steps.text: Line 23 makes a `Trip`, whose `nights` is 3. Line 24 makes a `TripEditor` with it, and line 25 makes a renderer.
Line 26 asks for the image, so SwiftUI runs the `body` of `TripEditor`. Line 19 makes a binding to `nights` of the trip, and gives it to an `Adder`.
The `Text` of `Adder` appears, so SwiftUI calls the closure of `onAppear`, which adds 1 to `count`. Writing the binding sets `nights` of the trip to 4.

end.text: The binding that `$trip.nights` made wrote to the trip itself, so the trip's `nights` changed.
